title: Yet Jansenius allows that sinners can do some good works, with Trent
source_text: XLVI. Quamvis autem vir ille nullum bonum opus agnoscat, nisi quod a charitate & fide quodammodo per dilectionem operante procedat, non negat tamen peccatores, hoc est, in peccato mortali constitutos, & qui nondum justificati sunt, & peccatorum suorum remissionem adepti, posse quaedam bona opera facere. Atque in eo subscribit Tridentinae Synodo, quae anathema dicit iis qui affirmant omnia opera quae ante justificationem fiunt, vera esse peccata. Si quis dixerit, inquit, Opera omnia quae ante justificationem fiunt, quacunque ratione facta sint, vera esse peccata, vel odium Dei mereri, anathema sit. Canone septimo Sessionis sextae.
pass_a_gloss: XLVI. Although however man that no good work acknowledges, unless what from charity & faith in a manner through love working proceeds, he denies not however sinners, that is, those set in mortal sin, and who are not yet justified, and have obtained remission of their sins, can do some good works. And in this he subscribes to the Tridentine Synod, which anathema says to those who affirm all works which before justification are done, to be true sins. If anyone shall have said, it says, That all works which are done before justification, in whatever way they be done, are true sins, or merit the hatred of God, let him be anathema. In canon seven of the sixth Session.
pass_b_english: Although that man acknowledges no good work except what proceeds from charity and from faith working in some way through love, he does not deny that sinners, that is, those in mortal sin, who have not yet been justified and obtained the forgiveness of their sins, can do some good works.

In this he subscribes to the Council of Trent, which pronounces anathema on those who affirm that all works done before justification are true sins: 'If anyone says that all works done before justification, in whatever way they are done, are true sins or merit God's hatred, let him be anathema.' Session 6, canon 7.

choices.why: Faith given by God's grace, not merely acquired belief in one God; Jansenius makes it the beginning of every good will.
